```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lmtest)
library(patchwork)
source("R/utils.R")
if (!file.exists("data/synthetic/non_linear_wq.csv")) {
  source("R/generate_synthetic_data.R")
}
non_linear_wq <- readr::read_csv("data/synthetic/non_linear_wq.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

Before reaching for one of the heavier models later on this site — [piecewise regression](piecewise-regression.qmd), [changepoint detection](changepoint-detection.qmd), [GAMs](gam.qmd) — a series deserves a simpler question: is it really nonlinear, or is it a straight line on the wrong scale? A simpler model that fits is generally the better model — fewer parameters to estimate, easier to explain, more likely to generalize beyond the data it was fit on. This chapter is that correction step.

By **correction** I mean a targeted change to how the straight-line model is set up — one that lets an ordinary linear fit describe a shape it couldn't handle as given, without switching to a different method.

Three such corrections exist: transform the response, feature-engineer the regressor, or change the link function (DSCI 561, DSCI 562). What follows is how to read a series' raw shape and residuals to tell which one applies, if any, using the five-part model from [The Regression Framework](regression-framework.qmd) to pin down where each acts.

## Matching the correction to the cause

A response with a restricted range — a concentration, which can't go negative — routinely needs some kind of correction before ordinary least squares is a defensible fit. A straight line fit to raw concentrations can even predict negative values within the record (Hirsch et al., 1991). Total Nitrogen is a case in point: flat for the first several years of the record, then rising. A straight line fit to it anyway captures neither stretch well.

```{r}
#| label: tn-raw-line
#| echo: false
tn_raw <- non_linear_wq |> filter(analyte == "Total Nitrogen")

ggplot(tn_raw, aes(year_frac, result)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Total Nitrogen — a straight line forced through a break in level",
       x = "Year", y = "result") +
  nlt_theme
```

The line is a compromise between two regimes it was never built to describe — too high early, too low late, too shallow in between. Which correction fixes that depends on where the problem actually sits.

Three techniques address these separately, and they are easy to conflate because more than one can involve the word "log" — but they are not interchangeable, and reaching for the wrong one leaves the real problem uncorrected.

$$ \underbrace{Y_i}_{\text{Response}} = \underbrace{\beta_0 + \beta_1 g_1(X_{i, 1}) + \ldots + \beta_k g_k(X_{i,k})}_{\text{Systematic Component}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_i}_{\text{Random Component}}. $$

Instead of a typical OLS model of `lm(result ~ year_frac)`, corrections could be made by:

-   **Transform the response** — `log(result)` instead of `result`. This changes OLS's estimand: the fitted mean becomes the conditional mean of `log(result)` instead of `result`. It's a data preparation step, done before the model ever sees the numbers.
-   **Feature-engineer the regressor** — for example, a hinge term `pmax(0, year_frac - c)` for a series whose slope itself changes partway through the record. This changes the shape of the systematic component while leaving the response and the link alone. Still OLS, still linear in the coefficients (see [The Regression Framework](regression-framework.qmd)) — just an additional regressor handed to `lm()`.
-   **Change the link function** — a generalized linear model with a log link function, $\log(E[Y\mid X]) = X\beta$. This changes how the mean relates to the linear predictor rather than the response itself.

The first and third both involve the word "log" applied to a concentration, but they aren't the same model: $E[\log(Y)\mid X]$ (log-transform-then-OLS) and $\log(E[Y\mid X])$ (a GLM log link) are different quantities and only coincide in special cases.

Concentration data is shaped by processes such as dilution and first-order removal that act as a proportional change on the current level rather than a fixed absolute amount (the multiplicative-process argument developed in full below), and that structure is what log-transform-then-OLS is built to estimate: it puts the model directly on the scale where a percentage-change process produces additive, symmetric noise.

A log-link GLM instead assumes the mean itself is multiplicative in the predictors while the noise stays additive on the raw scale — a different, also defensible assumption. This site uses **log-transform-then-OLS** because it matches the proportional-change process described above and expresses a trend as a percent per year, an approach long used in water-quality trend analysis (Hirsch et al., 1991). A log-link GLM remains a reasonable alternative.

The rest of this chapter works through these in order: how to tell, from the raw data and from residual diagnostics, whether a series needs the response transformed or the regressor feature-engineered; why log-transform-then-OLS in particular fits the multiplicative-process story environmental concentration data tends to follow; and, at the end, what a back-transformed fit estimates and how this approach relates to EPA's ProUCL guidance.

## Deciding between response-transform and the regressor-feature-engineering corrections

The response-transform and the regressor-feature-engineering questions get resolved separately, in a fixed order, because they fail differently.

### Step 1 — look at the raw shape before touching residuals

`log()` is a monotonic transform, so it can only re-scale curvature that's already headed one direction — it can straighten an accelerating or decaying curve, but it cannot introduce a bend, a peak, or a flattening that isn't there on the raw scale, and it cannot remove one that is. That splits raw-shape curvature into two cases:

-   **Monotonic curvature** that logging fixes: a quantity growing (or decaying) at a fixed percentage rate per period — i.e. exponential growth/decay, $y = Ae^{rt}$ — is curved on the raw scale but linear once logged: $\log(y) = \log(A) + rt$. Attenuation studies use this directly, deriving a first-order rate constant as the slope of log concentration against time (Newell et al., 2002). The panels below are a mock series at a 25%/year rate — unrealistically steep for real environmental chemistry, chosen purely to make the curvature-then-straightening visible.
-   **Non-monotonic shapes** — a plateau, a kink, a hump, or any curve that doesn't move consistently in one direction. These signal a need to feature-engineer the regressor instead of reaching for `log()`; no response transform fixes them.

```{r}
#| label: exp-raw-vs-log
#| message: false
#| echo: false
set.seed(42)
exp_demo <- tibble(year_frac = seq(0, 12, length.out = 60)) |>
  mutate(result = exp(log(15) + 0.25 * year_frac + rnorm(n(), sd = 0.1)))

p_raw <- ggplot(exp_demo, aes(year_frac, result)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Raw scale", x = "Year", y = "result") +
  nlt_theme

p_log <- ggplot(exp_demo, aes(year_frac, log(result))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Log scale", x = "Year", y = "log(result)") +
  nlt_theme

p_raw + p_log +
  plot_annotation(title = "Mock series, 25%/year growth — a curve that logging straightens")
```

On the raw scale the fitted line overshoots the middle of the record and undershoots both ends — a signature of forcing a straight line through what's actually an accelerating curve. On the log scale the same line runs through the data cleanly: this is the case Step 1 is checking `log(result)` for.

### Step 2 — fit the straight line anyway, and read the residuals, not the raw data

The **residual** for observation $i$ is the gap between what was observed and what the fitted line predicts, $\hat{e}_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$ — the vertical distance from a point to the fitted line, plotted directly in the systematic-vs-random-component figure in [The Regression Framework](regression-framework.qmd#a-model-has-five-moving-parts). A correctly specified model leaves residuals that look like patternless, constant-variance noise; how they depart from that is what tells you which correction is needed (DSCI 561, Lecture 7; STAT 501, Lesson 4).

Two different things can go wrong once the residuals are examined, and they matter for different reasons — one means the fitted line itself is in the wrong place, the other means the line might be fine but the uncertainty claimed around it isn't:

-   **A regressor problem.** Residuals show a pattern against the regressor: systematically high in some stretches and low in others, rather than scattered evenly. That means the fitted mean is the wrong shape: the line doesn't track the data's true curve, so the slope or rate read off it is biased rather than merely imprecise. This is the more serious failure, because it means the headline number is wrong (DSCI 561, Lecture 7).
-   **A distributional problem.** Residuals look patternless against the regressor — the mean structure is fine — but their spread grows with the fitted value, or their distribution departs from normal. Here the fitted mean can be trusted, but the confidence intervals and p-values built on top of it assume constant-variance, normally distributed noise, and stop being trustworthy once that assumption breaks. The point estimate can still be trusted; the confidence interval around it cannot (DSCI 561, Lecture 7).

```{r}
#| label: resid-pattern-mock
#| message: false
#| echo: false
set.seed(7)
n <- 100
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = n)

pattern_demo <- data.frame(x = x, resid = 2.5 * sin(x / 1.6) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3))
spread_demo <- data.frame(x = x, resid = rnorm(n, sd = 0.08 + 0.18 * x))

p_pattern <- ggplot(pattern_demo, aes(x, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Regressor problem", x = "regressor", y = "residual") +
  nlt_theme

p_spread <- ggplot(spread_demo, aes(x, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Distributional problem", x = "regressor", y = "residual") +
  nlt_theme

p_pattern + p_spread +
  plot_annotation(title = "Mock residual diagnostics — the two failure modes Step 2 separates")
```

The left panel is a mock: a smooth systematic wave, the smoother tracking well away from zero across stretches of the regressor — the signature of a mean structure that hasn't captured the true shape yet, no amount of response-transforming fixes this.

The right panel is also a mock: the smoother stays flat on zero (no shape has been missed), but the scatter visibly widens as the regressor increases — a distributional problem the response side of the model is meant to handle.

**Breusch-Pagan** and **Shapiro-Wilk** are formal tests for the distributional problem only — neither one checks whether the mean structure is right, so neither one can catch a regressor problem:

-   **Breusch-Pagan** tests $H_0$: the residual variance is constant across fitted values (homoscedasticity), by regressing the squared residuals on the regressor and testing whether that regression has any real explanatory power. A low p-value means the spread is changing — the residuals are fanning in or out (STAT 501, Lesson 7).
-   **Shapiro-Wilk** tests $H_0$: the residuals are drawn from a normal distribution, by comparing the ordered residuals against the values a normal distribution would be expected to produce. A low p-value means the residual distribution's shape — skew, heavy tails, multimodality — departs from normal (STAT 501, Lesson 7).

A regressor problem is best seen first: formal checks such as the lack-of-fit F-test exist, but they only give evidence against a straight line without saying which shape would fit (STAT 501, Lesson 2). Base R's `plot()` on a fitted model produces this directly, alongside the two panels that back up Breusch-Pagan and Shapiro-Wilk:

```{r}
#| label: tn-naive-diagnostics
fit_tn_naive <- lm(result ~ year_frac, data = tn_raw)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(fit_tn_naive, which = 1)
plot(fit_tn_naive, which = 2)
plot(fit_tn_naive, which = 3)
```

**Residuals vs Fitted** (`which = 1`) is the regressor-problem check — with a single regressor, fitted values are a monotonic function of it, so a pattern here is the same pattern a plot against the raw regressor would show; this is the one panel neither formal test looks at. **Normal Q-Q** (`which = 2`) is the visual companion to **Shapiro-Wilk**: points following the diagonal mean the residual distribution is close to normal, systematic curvature or S-shapes mean it isn't. **Scale-Location** (`which = 3`) is the visual companion to **Breusch-Pagan**: a flat trend means constant variance, an upward slope means it's fanning out. The first two panels are covered in DSCI 561 (Lecture 7) and STAT 501 (Lesson 4); the third is defined in the `plot.lm()` documentation.

### The bridge to a fully flexible regressor

A hinge function, $(x-c)_+ = \max(0, x-c)$, is the simplest possible case of feature-engineering the regressor: one knot, one new column, still fit by `lm()` (DSCI 562, Lecture 6). A generalized additive model's smooth term generalizes the same idea — many small basis functions instead of one hinge, combined additively, with a fitted penalty deciding how much of that flexibility survives rather than an analyst placing knots by eye (`mgcv` documentation, `?smooth.terms` and `?gam`; Simpson, 2018). The lineage is straight-line OLS $\to$ hinge-term feature engineering $\to$ many-basis-function smooth term, and it's the same "linear in the parameters" backbone the whole way — what changes across that lineage is how many, and how flexible, the basis functions handed to the fit are allowed to be.

## Log-transform-then-OLS for concentration data

### Why log a concentration in the first place

The **multiplicative** argument for environmental chemistry is that concentration data is strictly positive, and the processes that move it tend to act as a proportional change on the current level rather than a fixed absolute amount. Ott (1990) gives the physical basis for dilution: after a series of independent random dilutions, a concentration is the initial concentration multiplied by each dilution factor. Taking logs turns that product into a sum, so the logged concentration tends toward a normal distribution and the concentration toward a lognormal one: right-skewed on the raw scale, closer to symmetric once logged. Fitting `log(result)` rather than `result` is what typically fixes the two ordinary-least-squares assumptions raw concentration data tends to violate: **homoscedasticity** and **normality of residuals**. Transformations are a recognized response when normality or constant variance fails (Esterby, 1996; STAT 501, Lesson 9).

The skew is well documented for water-quality records: concentration data are typically positively skewed, with many values near zero and a few one or more orders of magnitude higher. Log transforms give more resistant and robust trend results for data that span more than an order of magnitude at a station (Hirsch et al., 1991).

Logging is a choice rather than an automatic step, and it depends on what the analysis has to report. It needs more caution when the result is an absolute concentration compared against a limit. This site logs every case study for consistency, which is a stated default rather than a finding about each series.

A coefficient estimated on `log(result)` is a rate in log-units per period, and back-transforming it, $(\exp(\hat\beta) - 1) \times 100\%$, gives the number that actually gets reported — a constant percentage rate of change in the median concentration, not a raw-unit slope (STAT 501, Lesson 9). This is the standard way log-scale trend slopes are expressed in water-quality work. Fitting a straight line to log concentrations is not a claim that the trend is exponential; it gives an exponential approximation to whatever the actual trend is (Hirsch et al., 1991).

### What a back-transformed fit estimates

The %/year rate above comes from the log-scale slope. Exponentiating a fitted log concentration, `exp(predict(fit))`, is a separate step with a different target: it estimates the median, or geometric mean, concentration rather than the arithmetic mean (STAT 501, Lesson 9; Ferguson, 1986). For right-skewed data the median sits below the mean, so the result understates the mean, and the gap widens as the scatter around the fit grows. Ferguson (1986) showed this for river load estimates built from log-log rating curves, where the underestimate can reach 50%.

The rates on this site describe proportional change in the median and are not used as absolute concentrations for a decision, so this bias does not affect them. If a raw-scale mean is the deliverable, two common options are a retransformation correction, such as Duan's (1983) smearing estimate, and a log-link GLM, such as a Gamma GLM, which models the raw-scale mean with no back-transformation step. Neither is best in all conditions. In Manning and Mullahy's (2001) health-economics study, log-OLS with smearing could be appreciably biased when the log-scale errors were heteroscedastic, and GLMs lost precision when those errors were heavy-tailed.

### How this relates to ProUCL

EPA's ProUCL software weighs a Gamma distribution against a lognormal one, but for a different problem than the one this chapter addresses (Singh, A. and Singh, A.K. 2015). That choice belongs to its Upper Confidence Limit (UCL), Upper Tolerance Limit, and background threshold value (BTV) modules, which compute a single population parameter from a time-collapsed sample, often with nondetects handled through Kaplan-Meier estimation. That is a fixed-in-time point estimate, not a conditional mean modeled as a function of a regressor, which is a different estimand than any method on this site targets (see [The Regression Framework](regression-framework.qmd)).

ProUCL's closer counterpart to this chapter is its Trend Analysis module, which fits OLS on the raw, untransformed response as a function of time and falls back to the nonparametric Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen tests when normal-residual assumptions fail. Like the methods on this site, it models a conditional mean as a function of a regressor. The companion `vignette-temporal-trends` project uses a similar cross-check, running log-transform-then-OLS alongside Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope.

ProUCL's guide advises avoiding data transformation (Section 4.2.2) for two main reasons: back-transformed statistics can carry large bias when used for cleanup decisions, and a log scale can hide outliers that represent contaminated locations. The bias concern is the back-transformation issue described above, and this site's %/year rates do not rely on a back-transformed concentration. The outlier concern still applies here, which is one reason to inspect raw-scale plots and to run Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope alongside log-OLS. A formal decision statistic, or a fitted value compared against a concentration limit, would need a different approach and is outside this site's scope of inference on the observed record.

## Summary

This chapter set up how to tell, before fitting anything more elaborate, whether a nonlinear-looking series is fixable with a correction to an ordinary straight-line fit rather than a genuinely different model: raw shape (Step 1) for whether the response needs `log()`, residual diagnostics (Step 2) for whether the regressor needs feature-engineering instead. For concentration data specifically, log-transform-then-OLS is the default: it matches the multiplicative-process story that dilution and first-order removal produce, and it expresses a trend as a percent per year. Exponentiating a log-scale fit estimates the median rather than the mean, which does not affect the case studies on this site, since results here are reported as %/year rates computed on the log scale, not used as absolute concentrations for a decision. A raw-scale mean or a formal decision statistic would call for a different approach.

With that diagnostic toolkit in place, the rest of this site stops asking whether a correction to a straight line is enough and starts fitting the methods built for series where it isn't — piecewise regression, changepoint detection, k-NN, LOESS, GAM, and GAMM, each demonstrated on a case study whose shape a response transform or a hand-engineered regressor can't capture.
